name: Migraine
overview: A migraine is usually a moderate or severe headache felt as a throbbing pain on one side of the head, often with feeling sick and sensitivity to light or sound. It is a common condition. Treatments can ease attacks and reduce how often they happen.
symptoms: Throbbing headache, often on one side
Sensitivity to light, sound or smells
Visual disturbances (aura) such as flashing lights or zigzags before the headache
Numbness, tingling or difficulty speaking during an aura
Tiredness before or after an attack
causes: Not fully understood, thought to involve changes in brain activity, nerves and blood vessels
Triggers such as stress, poor sleep, hormonal changes, missed meals, dehydration and some foods or alcohol
diagnosis: Migraine is diagnosed from the pattern of symptoms and an examination; scans are usually only needed if there are unusual features.
treatment: Painkillers such as paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin taken early in an attack
Triptan medicines prescribed by a doctor
Anti-sickness medicines
Preventive medicines if attacks are frequent
selfCare: Rest in a quiet, dark room during an attack
Keep a migraine diary to identify triggers
Avoid taking painkillers on too many days, which can cause medication-overuse headaches
whenToSeeDoctor: Frequent or severe migraines
Painkillers are not helping
Symptoms on most days
Migraine pattern changes
emergencySigns: Headache with stiff neck, fever, confusion or rash
Weakness on one side, slurred speech or face drooping

name: Tension-type headache
overview: Tension-type headaches are the most common kind of headache. They feel like a constant ache or pressure around the head, like a tight band. They are usually not serious and can be eased with simple painkillers and lifestyle changes.
symptoms: Pain on both sides of the head, face or neck
A feeling of tightness or pressure around the forehead
Tight or tender neck and shoulder muscles
Can usually carry on with normal activities
causes: Stress and anxiety
Poor posture
Lack of sleep
Skipping meals or not drinking enough fluids
Eye strain
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses tension-type headache from the symptoms and an examination.
treatment: Painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, used on a limited number of days
Treatment for frequent headaches, sometimes including preventive medicine
Physiotherapy or relaxation techniques
selfCare: Drink enough water and eat regularly
Improve posture and take screen breaks
whenToSeeDoctor: Headaches several times a week or getting worse
Painkillers are not helping
Headaches with other symptoms such as numbness or weakness
emergencySigns: Headache with stiff neck, fever or rash
Headache with weakness, confusion or slurred speech

name: Epilepsy
overview: Epilepsy is a condition where sudden bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause repeated seizures. It can start at any age. Most people can control their seizures with medicine.
symptoms: Strange sensations such as tingling, a rising feeling in the tummy or unusual smells
causes: Often no clear cause is found
Brain damage from stroke, head injury, infection such as meningitis, or a tumour
Genetic factors
riskFactors: Previous serious head injury or stroke
diagnosis: Epilepsy is diagnosed by a specialist using a description of the seizures, an EEG to record brain activity, and brain scans such as MRI.
treatment: Anti-seizure medicines
Surgery for some people
Special diets or nerve-stimulation devices in some cases
selfCare: Get enough sleep and avoid known triggers such as alcohol excess
Follow safety advice for bathing, swimming and driving
Share a seizure action plan with family and friends
prevention: Prevent head injuries, for example by wearing helmets
Take medicines regularly to reduce seizures
whenToSeeDoctor: Someone has a seizure for the first time
Seizures become more frequent or change
Side effects from medicines
You are planning pregnancy
emergencySigns: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Repeated seizures without recovering in between
Serious injury or breathing difficulty during a seizure

name: Parkinson's disease
overview: Parkinson's disease is a condition where parts of the brain become progressively damaged over many years, mainly affecting movement. There is no cure yet, but treatments help control symptoms and keep people active.
symptoms: Shaking (tremor), often starting in one hand
Loss of sense of smell, constipation, sleep problems and low mood
Memory or thinking problems later on
causes: Loss of nerve cells in the part of the brain that produces dopamine
Thought to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors
diagnosis: Parkinson's is diagnosed by a specialist from symptoms and an examination; there is no single test, and scans may be used to rule out other causes.
treatment: Medicines that replace or mimic dopamine
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy
Deep brain stimulation surgery for some people
selfCare: Stay as physically active as possible
Make the home safer to prevent falls
prevention: There is no proven way to prevent Parkinson's; regular exercise is good for overall health
whenToSeeDoctor: Tremor, stiffness or slowness of movement
Problems with balance or frequent falls
Changes in symptoms or medicine side effects
emergencySigns: A fall with a head injury or inability to get up

name: Dementia
overview: Dementia is a group of symptoms caused by diseases that damage the brain, affecting memory, thinking and daily life. It is not a normal part of ageing. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, followed by vascular dementia.
symptoms: Memory loss, especially of recent events
causes: Alzheimer's disease
Vascular dementia from reduced blood flow to the brain
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Frontotemporal dementia
riskFactors: High blood pressure, diabetes and smoking
diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms, does memory tests and blood tests, and may refer to a memory clinic for specialist assessment and brain scans.
treatment: Medicines that may help some symptoms of Alzheimer's or Lewy body dementia
Managing risk factors in vascular dementia
Cognitive stimulation and other activities
Support for carers and planning for the future
selfCare: Use reminders such as calendars and lists
Plan ahead, including legal and financial matters
prevention: Do not smoke and limit alcohol
whenToSeeDoctor: Memory problems that are getting worse
Concern from family or friends about memory or behaviour
Difficulty managing daily tasks
emergencySigns: Sudden confusion or rapid worsening (could be infection, stroke or delirium)
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems

name: Alzheimer's disease
overview: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. It gradually damages brain cells, affecting memory, thinking and behaviour. There is no cure, but treatments and support can help people live as well as possible.
causes: Build-up of abnormal proteins in the brain that damage nerve cells
A combination of age, genes, lifestyle and environment
riskFactors: Cardiovascular risk factors such as high blood pressure, smoking and diabetes
diagnosis: It is diagnosed through memory and thinking tests, a medical history, blood tests to rule out other causes, and sometimes brain scans at a specialist clinic.
treatment: Medicines that can help some symptoms for a time
Activities and therapies to support memory and wellbeing
Treatment for related problems such as low mood or sleep problems
Care and support planning
selfCare: Keep a routine and use memory aids
Make plans for future care while able
prevention: Healthy lifestyle: activity, not smoking, healthy diet
whenToSeeDoctor: Worsening memory problems
Family members notice changes in memory or behaviour
emergencySigns: Sudden confusion or a rapid change in behaviour

name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
overview: Multiple sclerosis is a lifelong condition where the immune system damages the protective coating around nerves in the brain and spinal cord. It can cause a wide range of symptoms, which vary between people. Treatments can reduce relapses and help manage symptoms.
symptoms: Vision problems, such as blurred vision or pain moving the eye
Bladder problems and difficulty thinking or concentrating
causes: The immune system attacking the myelin coating of nerves (an autoimmune condition)
A mix of genetic and environmental factors, including low vitamin D, smoking and past Epstein-Barr virus infection
diagnosis: MS is diagnosed by a neurologist using a neurological examination, an MRI scan, and sometimes a lumbar puncture.
treatment: Disease-modifying medicines to reduce relapses
Steroids to speed recovery from relapses
Treatments for specific symptoms such as fatigue, spasms or bladder problems
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation
prevention: There is no known way to prevent MS; not smoking may lower risk
whenToSeeDoctor: Vision problems, numbness, weakness or balance problems that last more than a day
New or worsening symptoms if you have MS
emergencySigns: Sudden weakness on one side, face drooping or slurred speech

name: Depression
overview: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days. It is a common mental health condition where low mood or loss of interest lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life. It is treatable, and most people recover with the right support.
symptoms: Loss of interest or enjoyment in things
Difficulty concentrating, or thoughts of self-harm or suicide
causes: Often a mix of factors rather than one cause
Stressful life events such as bereavement, divorce, job loss or illness
Family history and personality
Long-term health conditions, alcohol or drug use
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses depression by talking about symptoms, how long they have lasted and how they affect daily life.
treatment: Talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
Antidepressant medicines prescribed by a doctor
Combination of therapy and medicine
Specialist mental health care for severe depression
selfCare: Stay connected with people you trust
prevention: Seeking help early when mood is low
whenToSeeDoctor: Low mood or loss of interest lasting more than 2 weeks
Depression affecting work, relationships or daily life
Treatment is not helping
emergencySigns: Thoughts of ending your life or making plans to do so
Feeling unable to keep yourself safe

name: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
overview: Generalised anxiety disorder is a long-term condition where you feel anxious about many different things, most days, and find it hard to control the worry. It is common and treatable with talking therapies, medicines and self-help.
symptoms: Persistent worry that is hard to control
Physical symptoms such as a fast heartbeat, muscle tension, sweating or dizziness
causes: A mix of genetic, biological and life experience factors
Stressful or traumatic experiences
Long-term health conditions or alcohol and drug use
riskFactors: Heavy alcohol, caffeine or drug use
Other mental health conditions such as depression
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses GAD by asking about symptoms, how long they have lasted and how they affect daily life.
treatment: Talking therapies such as CBT
Guided self-help programmes
Medicines such as certain antidepressants, prescribed by a doctor
selfCare: Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
prevention: Healthy routines for sleep and exercise
whenToSeeDoctor: Anxiety is affecting daily life
Worry has lasted for several weeks or months
Self-help has not worked
emergencySigns: Chest pain or breathlessness that could be a heart problem (do not assume it is anxiety)

name: Panic disorder
overview: Panic disorder is an anxiety condition where you have regular, sudden panic attacks, often for no obvious reason, and worry about having more. Panic attacks feel frightening but are not dangerous in themselves. Treatment is effective.
symptoms: Sudden intense fear or a sense of doom
Shortness of breath or feeling of choking
Chest pain, nausea or tingling fingers
causes: A mix of genetic and life experience factors
Stressful life events
Sensitivity to the body's stress responses
riskFactors: Heavy caffeine, alcohol or drug use
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses panic disorder from your description of attacks, and may do tests to rule out heart or thyroid problems.
treatment: Talking therapies such as CBT
Medicines such as certain antidepressants, prescribed by a doctor
Self-help programmes
selfCare: During an attack, stay where you are and breathe slowly and deeply
Remind yourself that the attack will pass
whenToSeeDoctor: You have repeated panic attacks
Fear of attacks is stopping you doing things
You are avoiding places or situations
emergencySigns: Chest pain with sweating or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, especially if you have not had panic attacks before

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
overview: PTSD is a mental health condition that can develop after experiencing or witnessing a frightening or distressing event. People relive the trauma through flashbacks or nightmares and may feel constantly on guard. Effective treatments are available, even years after the event.
symptoms: Reliving the event through flashbacks, nightmares or intrusive images
Feeling on edge, irritable or easily startled
Physical symptoms such as sweating or pain when reminded
causes: Experiencing or witnessing traumatic events such as assault, accidents, abuse, war or disasters
Repeated trauma can lead to complex PTSD
riskFactors: Previous trauma or mental health problems
Lack of support after the event
Jobs with repeated exposure to trauma
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses PTSD by talking about symptoms and how long they have lasted, usually more than a month after the event.
treatment: Trauma-focused talking therapies such as trauma-focused CBT
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR)
Antidepressant medicines in some cases
selfCare: Keep regular routines for sleep, meals and exercise
Avoid using alcohol or drugs to cope
prevention: Getting support soon after a traumatic event
Seeking help early if symptoms persist
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms lasting more than 4 weeks after a traumatic event
Symptoms affecting daily life or relationships
emergencySigns: Feeling unable to keep yourself or others safe

name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
overview: ADHD is a condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control. Symptoms usually start in childhood and often continue into adulthood. Support, strategies and medicines can help people manage day-to-day life.
symptoms: Short attention span and being easily distracted
causes: Strong genetic component: it often runs in families
Differences in brain development and function
riskFactors: Premature birth or low birth weight
Exposure to alcohol, smoking or drugs during pregnancy
diagnosis: ADHD is diagnosed by a specialist such as a psychiatrist or paediatrician, based on a detailed assessment of symptoms over time and in different settings.
treatment: Medicines prescribed and monitored by a specialist
Parent training and education programmes
Talking therapies such as CBT
Support at school or work
prevention: There is no known way to prevent ADHD
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child may have ADHD
Symptoms are causing problems at school, work or in relationships
emergencySigns: Chest pain or fainting while taking ADHD medicine

name: Bipolar disorder
overview: Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings, from periods of depression to periods of very high mood and energy (mania or hypomania). It is a long-term condition, but treatment helps most people manage it well.
symptoms: Periods of depression: low mood, lack of energy, hopelessness
Periods of mania: feeling very happy or irritable, full of energy and ideas
Talking quickly and needing little sleep
Taking risks or making unusual decisions, such as spending sprees
Sometimes seeing or hearing things others do not (psychosis)
causes: A mix of genetic and environmental factors
Episodes can be triggered by stress, sleep disruption or substance use
diagnosis: Bipolar disorder is diagnosed by a psychiatrist after assessing mood patterns, symptoms and history over time.
treatment: Mood-stabilising medicines prescribed by a specialist
Talking therapies
Learning to recognise early warning signs of an episode
Hospital care during severe episodes
selfCare: Take medicines as prescribed even when well
prevention: Recognise and act on early warning signs
whenToSeeDoctor: Periods of very high or very low mood
Mood changes affecting work or relationships
Side effects of medicines
emergencySigns: Severe mania or psychosis putting you or others at risk

name: Insomnia
overview: Insomnia means regularly having problems getting to sleep or staying asleep, and feeling tired during the day. It is common and often improves with changes to sleep habits. Talking therapy for insomnia is the main long-term treatment.
symptoms: Waking several times in the night or too early
Feeling tired and irritable during the day
causes: Stress, anxiety or depression
Noise, light or an uncomfortable bedroom
Alcohol, caffeine or nicotine
Shift work or jet lag
Physical health problems or some medicines
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses insomnia by asking about sleep habits and daily routine, sometimes using a sleep diary.
treatment: Improving sleep habits
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)
Treating any underlying cause
Sleeping tablets only rarely and for a short time
selfCare: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day
Relax before bed and avoid screens
Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool
Avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals late in the evening
Exercise regularly, but not just before bed
whenToSeeDoctor: Sleep problems lasting more than a few weeks despite changes
Insomnia affecting daily life
Loud snoring or gasping during sleep

name: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)
overview: OCD is a mental health condition where a person has unwanted, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and feels driven to carry out repetitive actions (compulsions) to relieve the anxiety. It can be very time-consuming, but treatment helps most people.
symptoms: Unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images or urges
Fear of contamination, harm or things not being right
Repetitive behaviours such as cleaning, checking or counting
Mental rituals such as repeating words
Spending a lot of time on rituals and feeling distressed
causes: Not fully understood
Genetics, brain differences and life experiences all play a part
riskFactors: Certain personality traits such as perfectionism
diagnosis: OCD is diagnosed by a GP or mental health professional through a conversation about thoughts, behaviours and their impact.
treatment: Talking therapy: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
Antidepressant medicines in some cases
Specialist services for severe OCD
selfCare: Practise resisting compulsions gradually with support
Look after sleep, activity and stress
prevention: Seeking help early can stop OCD getting worse
whenToSeeDoctor: Obsessions or compulsions are taking up a lot of time or causing distress
OCD is affecting work, school or relationships

name: Schizophrenia
overview: Schizophrenia is a long-term mental health condition that affects how a person thinks, feels and perceives reality. People may experience hallucinations or delusions. With treatment and support, many people manage their symptoms and live well.
symptoms: Hallucinations: hearing or seeing things others do not
Delusions: strong beliefs not shared by others
Losing interest in everyday activities and withdrawing from others
causes: A combination of genetic and environmental factors
Stressful life events or drug use, such as cannabis, can trigger it in people at risk
riskFactors: Heavy cannabis or other drug use, especially in adolescence
diagnosis: Schizophrenia is diagnosed by a psychiatrist after a detailed assessment of symptoms over time, with tests to rule out other causes.
treatment: Antipsychotic medicines
Talking therapies such as CBT for psychosis and family intervention
Support from community mental health teams
Hospital care during severe episodes
selfCare: Keep regular routines and stay physically active
Stay in contact with your care team
prevention: Avoiding cannabis and drug use may lower risk
Early treatment of psychosis improves outcomes
whenToSeeDoctor: Hearing or seeing things others do not
Unusual beliefs or withdrawal noticed by others
Side effects of medicines
emergencySigns: Risk of harm to self or others
Severe confusion or inability to look after oneself
